title: The lost son (Kern ch. 4)
hook: a son who ran away returns as a poor laborer; his rich father slowly raises him until he can tell him the truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputra, the disciple who feared he'd been left out, was told by name that he would become a Buddha. Your line: he too will wake. Did you tell someone what you see them becoming? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

This time the Buddha isn't the one telling the story. In chapter four of the Lotus, it's the disciples who stand up. They have just watched Sariputra receive his promise, and they are amazed, because they had stopped expecting anything more. Subhuti and Kasyapa are among them. They bow and say: let us tell you a story, to show what has happened to us. And the story they tell is about a runaway. Today: the lost son.
screen: `THE DISCIPLES STAND UP.` → `LET US TELL YOU A STORY.` → `A STORY ABOUT A RUNAWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the two lives. In Kern's telling, a young man leaves his father and wanders off to other lands, getting poorer as the years go by. Meanwhile his father searches for him, settles in a city, and becomes very rich, with storehouses, servants and a crowd at his door. All the while he thinks of his son and tells no one. Second, the gate. One day the son, now a beggar looking for work, drifts to his father's house. He sees a great man on a throne, surrounded by attendants, and doesn't recognize him. This must be a king, he thinks. If I stay, they'll seize me and force me to work. He runs. The father knows him at once and sends servants after him, and the son is so terrified that he faints. So the father has water sprinkled on his face and lets him go, saying nothing. Third, the slow way. The father sends two men who look as poor as the son to offer him a job: clearing away the dirt heap, for good wages. The son takes it. Then the father takes off his fine clothes and jewels, puts on dirty work clothes, picks up a basket, and goes to work beside him. He talks to him. He tells him to stay, raises his wages, and starts calling him son. Even so, the son still thinks of himself as a hired hand. Over time the father gives him charge of the whole household and its treasure, and still the son lives in his small hut. Fourth, the truth. At last, when the father is near the end of his life, he calls together his relatives, the king and the townspeople, and announces: this is my son, who ran away long ago. Everything I have is his. The father had the truth the whole time. What he waited for was a son who could hear it without running. Tomorrow, the disciples explain who the son is.
screen: `A RUNAWAY GROWS POOR.` · `HE SEES A KING, AND RUNS.` · `THE FATHER IN WORK CLOTHES.` · `THIS IS MY SON.` · then, large: `THE LOST SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: be patient with one slow learner. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone who isn't ready yet: a child, a coworker, a parent learning a phone, maybe yourself learning something hard. Notice how much you'd like to say the whole truth right now. Then think of the father, setting down his jewels and picking up a basket. What would it look like to work beside this person instead of above them? Let one small picture come. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.

The lost son. The disciples' parable in chapter four: a runaway who returns too poor and frightened to know his father, and a father who raises him step by step until the truth can be told. Today's word.
Your line: the lost son. Today, when someone isn't ready for the whole thing, give them one step and stand beside them while they take it. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: The parable of the lost son, told by the senior disciples in chapter four of the Lotus Sutra, is retold in East Asian Buddhist teaching as a picture of the Buddha's patient skillful means.

fork.setup: you are the rich father. your son has finally come to your gate, and fainted from fear at the sight of you. what do you do?
options: tell him at once that he is your son
sprinkle water on his face and let him go
keep him locked in the house until he understands
fork.reveal: the father lets him go without a word, then sends poor-looking men to offer him a humble job, and begins the slow way.

original.note: Sanskrit: inclination, disposition, trusting resolve; the name of chapter four in Kern's Sanskrit text.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a rich family reunion.
what it means: the disciples see themselves in the son, raised step by step by a patient father until they can hear the whole truth.
what a scholar hears: chapter four is named for adhimukti, disposition, because the father fits each step to what the son can accept, the upaya of chapter two in a family story.

notes: Chapter 4 parable paraphrased from Kern (SBE XXI, 1884); nothing quoted.

Check: the tellers (Kern names Subhuti, Maha-Katyayana, Maha-Kasyapa and Maha-Maudgalyayana; only Subhuti and Kasyapa named here); the son's flight and fainting; the water sprinkled on his face; two poor-looking messengers; the dirt-heap job; the father in dirty clothes; the hut; the announcement before relatives and the king. Kern gives the son's years away and other figures; omitted under the claims rule.
The practice and teach avoid any comparison with the Gospel parable of the prodigal son; editor should keep it that way.
Original: Adhimukti (अधिमुक्ति) as chapter-four title; Keeper to confirm.
